historical_record.description: St. John's German Evangelical Church moved an 1860s-era former Presbyterian church onto the lot, bringing it from Franklin and Vallejo streets, where it had stood for sixteen years.
St. John's dedicated the relocated and rehabilitated church building.
Less than a month after its dedication, St. John's refurbished church was destroyed in the earthquake and fire.
St. John's contracted for a new two-story wood-frame church on the site at a cost of $9,850.
The cornerstone of the new church was laid, consecrating the site.

Built in 1907 as St. John's German Evangelical Church, and later the home of the Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples, reputed to be the first intentionally interracial congregation of its kind in the United States. It is a designated city landmark.
St. John's German Evangelical Church held its first service in the newly built church, its second dedication on this lot.
St. John's German Evangelical Church, here since 1907, gave up the building.
Banks turned down the interracial congregation for a mortgage on the building, one calling it too bad a risk, so the church paid with a private loan instead.
The Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples bought the church for $30,000, plus $6,000 for repairs, ending five years of moving between rented quarters.
A thirteen-member church delegation, led by Sue Bailey Thurman and including the church's quintet, sailed from New York to attend UNESCO's Fourth General Conference in Paris unofficially.
With the purchase loan repaid, the mortgage was burned at a Sunday service before about 500 people.
Howard Thurman left the church to become dean of Marsh Chapel at Boston University, the first Black dean at a predominantly white university.
Century Stained Glass Studio rebuilt one of the sanctuary's leaded glass windows on the south side.
Century Stained Glass Studio again worked on the sanctuary's south-side leaded glass window.
The foundation was underpinned.
Dry rot was repaired, the bell tower's south wall was partly seismically retrofitted, and a ramp and new exit door were added at the front; the work was signed off in 2012.
The church revived its theatre productions, among them the West Coast premiere of the play "Lady Day in Love".
The church was re-roofed.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 309, The Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples.
